Related Publications

title: Scoring 2: Special Cases
text: In this document, scoring for selected cases and scoring for external task set are presented. We still use the scoring() function, but we will need to provide additional information in these scenarios.

title: Scoring 2: Special Cases
text:
Preparation
Load required packages.

library(tidyverse)
library(bspam)

Again, the scoring requires calibration results saved as an object. If a calibration result object has not been saved, run a calibration process, such as:

MCEM_run1 <- fit.model(data = passage2,
                       person.id = "id.student",
                       task.id = "id.passage",
                       max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                       obs.counts = "wrc",
                       time = "sec",
                       reps.in = 50)

title: Scoring 2: Special Cases
text:
Scoring for Selected Cases
If the scoring for only selected cases are desired, a list of cases needs to be provided by the cases = argument. The list of cases has to be a one-variable data frame with a variable name cases. The format of case values should be: personid_occasion. This one-variable data frame can be created manually, just like shown below. Also, it can be generated by the get.cases() function.

sample.cases <- data.frame(cases = c("2033_fall", "2043_fall", "2089_fall"))
WCPM_sample <- scoring(calib.data = MCEM_run1, 
                       data = passage2,
                       person.id = "id.student",
                       occasion = "occasion",
                       group = "grade",
                       task.id = "id.passage",
                       max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                       obs.counts = "wrc",
                       time = "sec",
                       cases = sample.cases,
                       est = "eap", 
                       se = "analytic",
                       type = "orf")

title: Scoring 2: Special Cases
text:
Scoring for External Task Set
Also, we can specify a set of tasks (i.e., passages) to scale the WCPM scores. If WCPM scores are scaled with a set of passages that is different from the set of passages the student read, the set of passages is referred to as an external passage set for the ORF assessment context, or external task set in general.
The use of an external passage set is particularly important in the context of ORF assessment to make the estimated WCPM scores to be comparable between students who read different sets of passages, as well as within students for longitudinal data, where a student is likely to read different sets of passages.

WCPM_sample_ext1 <- scoring(calib.data = MCEM_run1, 
                            data = passage2,
                            person.id = "id.student",
                            occasion = "occasion",
                            group = "grade",
                            task.id = "id.passage",
                            max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                            obs.counts = "wrc",
                            time = "sec",
                            cases = sample.cases, 
                            external = c("32004","32010","32015","32016","33003","33037"),
                            est = "eap", 
                            se = "analytic",
                            type = "orf")
summary(WCPM_sample_ext1)

title: Scoring 2: Special Cases
text:
Scoring by Bayesian Approach
A fully Bayesian approach can also be used as an estimator in the scoring() function. Note that if est="bayes" is specified, there is no need to use the se= argument. By default, the standard deviations of the posterior distributions are reported as the standard errors, along with 95% high density intervals, which is analogous to 95% confidence intervals. Here is an example of using the fully Bayesian approach for estimating WCPM scores from the same external passages used in the previous example.

WCPM_sample_ext1_bayes <- scoring(calib.data=MCEM_run1, 
                                  data = passage2,
                                  person.id = "id.student",
                                  occasion = "occasion",
                                  group = "grade",
                                  task.id = "id.passage",
                                  max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                                  obs.counts = "wrc",
                                  time = "sec",
                                  cases = sample.cases, 
                                  external = c("32004","32010","32015","32016","33003","33037"),
                                  est = "bayes",
                                  type = "orf")
summary(WCPM_sample_ext1_bayes)

title: Data Requirements
text:
Data Preparation
It is required that the data are prepared as a long-format data, where each row is data for a unique case, namely, a specific task from a specific person in a specific testing occasion. In the context of ORF assessment, each row is data for a specific passage from a specific student in a specific testing occasion. A data file can be prepared in any file format that is readable into R.
For example, a CSV formatted data can be read into R by using the read.csv() function that is part of the base packages. Also, data files in some statistical software formats can be read in to R with functions in packages, such as the haven package. For example, read_spss() function can be used to read in an SPSS formatted data file into R.
Data should minimally contain the following 5 variables:
(1) individual ID,
(2) task ID,
(3) the maximum number of attempts in the task,
(4) the number of successes in the task, and
(5) the time took to complete the task.
Variable names and the order of the variables can be flexible in the data frame. When running functions in this package, variable names for required variables need to be specified, as shown in examples shown in the Tutorial section.


Example Data sets in bspam R Package
The bspam R package comes with several example data sets in the ORF assessment context. In the context of an ORF assessment, a task is a passage given to the student to read aloud, and an attempt is student’s reading on a word in the passage, which is scored correct (i.e., success) or not. Accordingly, the number of successes in the task is the number of words correctly read in the passage.
For example, the data set passage2 is a passage-level student data and consisted of reading accuracy and time data for 12 passages from 85 students. Although the 85 students were assigned to all 12 passages, the number of passages read by the 85 students varied from 2 to 12 passages. The number of students per passage were between 59 to 79. This is a small subset of the data collected by Nese and Kamata (2014-2018).
A list of all data sets in the bspam package is as follows.







Data Object Name
Brief Description




passage2
Passage-level ORF example data


sentence.level.data
Sentence-level/testlet ORF example data


sentence.cens.low
Sentence-level example data with low censoring


sentence.cens.high
Sentence-level example data with high censoring



The package also includes two calibration output objects. These objects can be directly used in the scoring() function bypassing the calibration step. They are potentially useful for those who wish to manually produce a calibration output object for scoring, such as in a simulation study.







Output Object Name
Brief Description




passage.calib.mcem
Example MCEM calibration output object with passage2 data


passage.calib.bayes
Example Bayesian calibration output object with passage2 data

title: What is bspam?
text: bspam is named after Speed-Accuracy Psychomeric Modeling for Binomial count outcome data. It is an R package that contains functions to fit the speed-accuracy latent variable psychometric model for repeatedly measured count outcome data (Potgieter, Kamata & Kara, 2017; Kara, Kamata, Potgieter & Nese, 2020; Potgider, Kamata, Kara, & Qiao, 2025), which is an extension of van der Linden (2007). In the bspam model, the accuracy and speed are modeled by a binomial count and a log-normal latent variable models, respectively. It also estimates speed and accuracy latent factor scores as described in Potgieter, Qiao, Kamata, and Kara (2024) and Kara, Kamata, Potgieter, and Nese (2020). For example, the use of this modeling technique allows model-based calibration and scoring for oral reading fluency (ORF) assessment data, estimating model-based WCPM scores.

title: Testlet Model
text: When ORF data are collected at the sentence level, sentences are nested within passages and may exhibit local dependence. In this case, a testlet-version of the model can be fitted and scored using bspam.

title: Testlet Model
text:
Example Data Set
The example data set sentence.level.data is a sentence-level student data and consisted of reading accuracy and time data for 4 passages from 58 students. The 4 passages were consisted of 4 to 8 sentences, totaling 23 sentences. All 58 students read all 4 passages completely. This is a small subset of the data collected by Nese and Kamata (2014-2018).

title: Testlet Model
text:
Preparation
Load required packages.

library(tidyverse)
library(bspam)

title: Testlet Model
text:
Calibration
We can use the fit.model() function in a similar way to the passage-level calibration. Two additional required arguments to include for testlet model calibration are sub.task.ed = and testlet = TRUE.

Testlet_run <- 
  fit.model(data        = sentence.level.data,
            person.id   = "id.student",
            task.id     = "id.passage",
            sub.task.id = "id.sentence",
            max.counts  = "numwords.sent",
            obs.counts  = "wrc",
            time        = "sec",

Scoring
The scoring by the MAP can be done for this data set by:

Testlet_scoring <- 
  scoring(calib.data = Testlet_run,
          data = sentence.level.data,
          person.id = "id.student",
          task.id = "id.passage",
          sub.task.id = "id.sentence",
          obs.counts = "wrc", 
          max.counts = "numwords.sent",
          time = "sec",
          type = "orf",
          testlet = TRUE,
          censoring = TRUE)

title: Tutorial: Introduction
text:
The bspam package contains many functions, where users may not need to directly specify in their code to analyze their data. A list of functions that are essential or potentially useful to typical users are provided below.







Function
Purpose




fit.model()
Estimate task parameters by MCEM or Bayesian estimation


scoring()
Estimate latent factor scores and model-based WCPM scores


summary()
Produce summary output for calibration and scoring results


get.cases()
Generate a list of person-by-occasion case identifiers


plot.task()
Visualize task parameter estimates


plot.person()
Visualize person-level score estimates


plot.information()
Visualize the information function for task parameters



Other functions in the package are mostly dependents for these key functions, such as run.mcem(), run.scoring(), bayes(), and bayes.wcpm(). Please refer to the package manual for details of other functions available in the package.

title: Data Exploration
text:
Load Packages
First, we load required packages, including the bspam and tidyverse packages. We also load the example data set passage2.

library(tidyverse)
library(bspam)
data("passage2")

title: Data Exploration
text:
Data Exploration
The data set passage2 is a passage-level student data on ORF assessment and consisted of reading accuracy and time data for 12 passages from 85 students.Although the 85 students were assigned to all 12 passages, the number of passages read by the 85 students varied from 2 to 12 passages. The number of students per passage were between 59 to 79. This is a small subset of the data collected by Nese and Kamata (2014-2018).
The seven variables in the data set includes:


id.student: individual ID.
occasion: timing of the assessment.
grade: grade level of the student.
id.passage: passage ID.
numwords.pass: the number of words in the passage.
wrc: the number of correctly read words.
sec: the time took to read the passage in seconds.

Some descriptive statistics are provided below. First, data were aggregated for each of the 12 passages as follows.

passage2 %>% 
  group_by(id.passage) %>% 
  mutate(rate.wrc = wrc/numwords.pass,
         sec.per10 = sec/numwords.pass*10) %>% 
  summarise(n.students = n(),
            numwords.pass = unique(numwords.pass),
            mean.wrc = mean(wrc),
            mean.sec = mean(sec),
            mean.rate.wrc = mean(rate.wrc),
            mean.sec.per10 = mean(sec.per10)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%

title: Plotting Results
text:
Preparation
Load required packages.

library(tidyverse)
library(bspam)

Functions to plot results read an object that contains calibration results or scoring results.
The scoring requires calibration results saved as an object.

MCEM_run1 <- fit.model(data = passage2,
                       person.id = "id.student",
                       task.id = "id.passage",
                       max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                       obs.counts = "wrc",
                       time = "sec",
                       reps.in = 50)


WCPM_all <- scoring(calib.data=MCEM_run1, 
                    data = passage2,
                    person.id = "id.student",
                    occasion = "occasion",
                    group = "grade",
                    task.id = "id.passage",
                    max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                    obs.counts = "wrc",
                    time = "sec",
                    est = "map", 
                    se = "analytic",
                    type="orf")

title: Plotting Results
text:
Plot Calibration Results

plot.task(MCEM_run1, parameter = "a", sort = TRUE)

Plot Scoring Results
Estimated latent factor scores or model-based WCPM scores can be plotted along with their standard errors.

plot.person(WCPM_all, parameter = "wcpm", show.se = TRUE)





Estimcated model-based WCPM scores can be plotted along with observed WCPM scores.

plot.wcpm(WCPM_all)

title: Scoring 1: Basics
text:
In order to estimate latent factor scores and/or WCPM scores, the scoring() function needs to be run.
Note that we use the output object MCEM_run from the previous passage calibration phase. By default (type = "general"), only factor scores (\(\theta\) and \(\tau\)) and their standard errors are reported. By providing an argument type = "orf", WCPM scores and their standard errors are also reported. Also, WCPM scores and/or factor scores, and their standard errors will be estimated for all cases in the data by default.
There are several estimator options and standard error estimation options. Options for the estimator are: maximum likelihood (MLE), maximum a posteriori (MAP), expected a posteriori (EAP), and fully Bayesian approach. Otions for the standard errors are: analytically derived Delta method and simulation-based bootstrap method.

title: Getting Started
text:
Installation
To install the bspam package, follow the steps below.
1. Install remotes package, by running the following R code.

if(!requireNamespace("remotes", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("remotes") 

2. Install bspam by running the following R code.

remotes::install_github("kamataak/bspam")



Optional
bspam can implement a fully Bayesian approach for the calibration of model parameters and scoring by using JAGS or Stan. If you desire to use the fully Bayesian estimation, please download JAGS and Stan software on your computer.
To download and install JAGS, download the installation file from https://sourceforge.net/projects/mcmc-jags/files/JAGS/ as per operating system requirements and follow the installation steps. bspam internally uses runjags package as an interface to JAGS. runjags package needs to be installed separately once JAGS is installed.
Stan can be installed by following the steps explained here: https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started. Note that these steps show the installation of RStan, which bspam uses as an internal package to run Stan code. Please follow the installation steps carefully along with recommended versions of R and RStudio to prevent any issues releated to running Stan with bspam.

title: Scoring for Truncated Response Data
text: In some circumstances, a test may be designed as a speeded test, such that many examinees do not complete all the tasks in the test. For example, a traditional administration of the ORF test limits the student 60 seconds to read aloud the given passage, which is typically consisted of 250 words. In this case, many students do not finish reading the entire passage. The bspam R package can score such a data set by the censored model both for the regular and the testlet models.

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text: As an example of task calibration, this document demonstrates the passage parameter calibration using passage2 example ORF data. Note that a passage is a task in the ORF context.

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text:
Load Packages
First, we load required packages tidyverse and bspam, and the example data set passage2.

library(tidyverse)
library(bspam)
data("passage2")

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text:
Passage Calibration
We will use the fit.model() function with the default estimation method, which is the Monte Carlo EM algorithm described in Potgieter et al. (2025).
The fit.model() function requires several arguments. The description of the arguments are summarized in the table below.

Table 2-1. Key Arguments for the fit.model( ) Function for Fitting Task-Level model







Arguments
Required
Description




data
Yes
The name of the data-frame object


person.id
Yes
Quoted variable name in data for the unique person identifier. In the ORF context, typically student ID.


task.id
Yes
Quoted variable name in data for the task identifier. In ORF context, passage ID.


max.count
Yes
Quoted variable name in data for the number of attempts in the task. In ORF context, the number of attempted words in the passage.


obs.count
Yes
Quoted variable name in data for the number of successful attempts in the task. In ORF context, the number of correctly read words.


time
Yes
Quoted variable name in data for the time in seconds to complete the task. In ORF context, time to complete reading the passage.


occasion
Optional
Quoted variable name in data for indicating different measurement occasions.


group
Optional
The variable name in the data for indicating different groups of individuals, such as grade levels.


k.in
Optional
The number of EM imputations. The default is k.in = 5 .


reps.in
Optional
The number of Monte-Carlo iterations. The default is reps.in = 2 .


est
Optional
Quoted string, indicating the choice of the estimator. It has to be "mcem" or "bayes". Default is "mcem" .


se
Optional
Quoted string, indicating the choice of the standard errors. It has to be one of "none" , "analytic" , or "bootstrap" . Default is "none" .


verbose
Optional
If TRUE, the summary will be output. Default is FALSE.



With minimally required arguments, the specification for the fit.mode() function to fit the passage2 data look like as follows. Note that the only optional argument included is reps.in = 50 where the number of Monte-Carlo iterations is set to 50, rather than 2 by default.

MCEM_run1 <- fit.model(data = passage2,
                       person.id = "id.student",
                       task.id = "id.passage",
                       max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                       obs.counts = "wrc",
                       time = "sec",
                       reps.in = 50)

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text:
Interpretations
Under the $task.param, estimated passage parameters are outputted. Accuracy parameters are a and b, where a is the discrimination parameter and b is the difficulty parameter, similar to the interpretations of 2-parameter item response theory (IRT) model parameters. Thus, a higher b indicates easier passage to read more accurately, and a higher a indicates a passage with higher association the probability of reading words correctly and the latent trait of accuracy. On the other hand, alpha and beta are time-intensity parameters (or time-difficulty) of passages. A higher beta indicates a passage which takes more time, given the same latent speed ability. It is in the scale of the logarithm of seconds to read per 10 words.
Based on the result, Passage 32010 had the lowest b, indicating the easiest in accuracy, while Passages 33003 had the highest b, indicating the hardest in accuracy. These are consistent with the descriptive statistics presented above. On the other hand, based on the estimated beta, Passage 23019 was among the easiest in time intensity, while Passage 32016 was most difficult in time intensity, again, consistent with the descriptive statistics above.

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text:
Note
By default, the standard errors for the model parameters are not estimated. This will allow one to increase the number of Monte-Carlo iterations reps.in to improve the quality of the model parameter estimates, while minimizing the computation time. The number of reps.in should be 50 to 100 in realistic calibrations. Also note that k.in is the number of imputations for the MCEM algorithm, where the default is 5. Note that SE’s for model parameters are not required for running the scoring() function to estimate latent factor scores and WCPM scores in the next step. If standard errors for model parameters are desired, an additional argument se = "analytic" or se = "bootstrap" needs to be added to the fit.model() function.

title: Task Calibration for Task-Level Data
text:
Bayesian Calibration
Task/passage calibration can also be performed by providing est = "bayes" argument. This will implement a fully Bayesian approach through Gibbs sampling by JAGS or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo by Stan. Currently, bspam uses Stan with complete data, that is, if all individuals have data on all tasks. Otherwise, bspam uses JAGS because it provides faster computations with missing observations. Note that bspam runs JAGS in its auto mode, which does not require the user to supply any specifications typically required for the Bayesian estimation, including the number of iterations and monitoring convergence. The standard deviations of the posterior distributions are reported in lieu of the standard errors. A specification for the fit.model( ) function can look like as follows.

Bayes_run <- fit.model(data = passage2,
                       person.id = "id.student",
                       task.id = "id.passage",
                       max.counts = "numwords.pass",
                       obs.counts = "wrc",
                       time = "sec",
                       est = "bayes",
                       verbose=TRUE)
